rationale: One three-case errno table for a syscall that already exists, with the defect an argument-validation ordering bug rather than a missing feature. timerfd_gettime01 asserts exactly three cases: EBADF when fd is -1, EFAULT when curr_value points at an unmapped address, and EINVAL when fd is a valid fd that is not a timerfd. Reading kernel/src/syscall/timerfd_gettime.rs, all three pieces of machinery are present but sequenced wrongly. The handler opens with a NULL check at lines 17-19 that returns EINVAL for itimerspec_addr == 0, and that check runs *before* the fd is ever looked up. Two of the test's three cases pass NULL as curr_value (tst_its_get(NULL) returns NULL, per include/tst_timer.h:190), so the EBADF case (fd = -1, its = NULL) and the EINVAL-wrong-fd-type case (fd = a regular file opened via SAFE_OPEN, its = NULL) both hit that early return. The EBADF case therefore reports EINVAL where Linux reports EBADF -- Linux resolves the fd first and only then touches the user pointer. The remaining pieces are already correct: raw_fd.try_into() yields EBADF for negative fds (kernel/src/fs/file/file_table.rs:93-95), get_file supplies EBADF for unallocated fds, the downcast_ref::<TimerfdFile>() at line 25 already yields EINVAL for a non-timerfd, and write_val at line 33 already yields EFAULT for a bad address. So the fix is reordering the fd resolution ahead of the pointer check, and dropping or relocating the hand-rolled NULL special case -- a handful of lines in one 36-line file, no new subsystem and no data-structure change. Sibling coverage confirms the surrounding infrastructure works: timerfd01 and timerfd02 are already enabled in all.txt, and this run's probe boot measured timerfd_settime01 and timerfd_settime02 passing in Asterinas, so TimerfdFile, timerfd_create, and the clock plumbing underneath are all sound and only the gettime argument-check order is wrong. Measured, not assumed: timerfd_gettime01 passes on the host with the pinned LTP 20260529 binary, and fails in Asterinas at base e8f2b9ca6 in this run's single probe boot of 49 candidates. Ground earlier rounds did not cover: rounds 1-4 (run-7UHmXC fsync03, run-atDPcd dup02, run-iIbwju clock_getres01, run-rVlQYu epoll_ctl02) all took all.txt entries but none touched timerfd, and every candidate in this run's probe batch was absent from the shared select.cache, so this round measured fresh ground rather than re-probing theirs. Preferred over the other clean failures this run measured. Rejected setpriority01/02 as a permissions and semantics cluster rather than one check: setpriority01 needs useradd plus setuid and a full -20..19 sweep where getpriority must read back exactly what setpriority wrote, which the implementation cannot satisfy because sys_set_priority clamps prio into range instead of rejecting, and kernel/src/syscall/set_priority.rs carries a standing FIXME that the per-process nice value is not the scheduler's source of truth; setpriority02 additionally needs ESRCH for a missing target, EACCES, and EPERM distinguished under an unprivileged uid. Rejected sched_getattr01 because it requires SCHED_DEADLINE -- it calls sched_setattr with sched_policy = SCHED_DEADLINE and brks out if that fails, so passing it means implementing a deadline scheduling class, not a check. Rejected semget02 as a System V IPC permission-model gap needing EACCES under setuid plus SEMMSL limit enforcement across six cases. Rejected mincore01, splice01/02, and tee01 because SYS_MINCORE, SYS_SPLICE, SYS_TEE, and SYS_VMSPLICE are all absent from kernel/src/syscall/arch/x86.rs and their probes came back broken rather than failing, so each is a whole missing syscall plus a broken-setup tangle. Rejected the socket cluster (accept01/02/03, connect01/02, recv01, recvfrom01, send01/02, sendto01/02, recvmsg01, sendmsg01, getsockopt01, setsockopt01/04) because most came back broken rather than as clean assert failures, which points at harness or setup problems that would have to be untangled before any kernel defect is visible, and prior runs already hit the same wall on shutdown01/02 and getsockname01. Rejected ioctl01 and ioctl07 as tty-dependent (ioctl02 needs an explicit -d tty device even on the host), and clock_settime01 as wall-clock mutation that overlaps the vdso and clock work run-iIbwju already diagnosed. Also considered and rejected the ext2/exfat blocked pools: all.txt is the higher-priority pool, and their only distinct entries are renameat201/renameat202, which need RENAME_EXCHANGE implemented in both filesystems -- a feature gap, not a localized defect.
notes: Pool entry is line 1715 of all.txt, exactly '# timerfd_gettime01'. Default run configuration -- entry comes from all.txt, so no CONFORMANCE_TEST_WORKDIR override and run_vars is empty. Probe boot used RELEASE=1 NETDEV=user and completed in 2m48s. This run's probe measured 7 already-passing still-blocked entries worth a cheap future round: getsockopt02, madvise03, sched_getattr02, rt_sigtimedwait01, sendmsg02, timerfd_settime01, timerfd_settime02 -- all recorded as stale-entry records in select.cache. Note timerfd_settime02 passed but took 2m30s of the boot, so it is slow rather than broken. Host tbroke results for eventfd01-05, ftruncate04_64, sched_getscheduler01, writev03, clock_gettime02/03, sched_rr_get_interval01-03 and the setsockopt05-10 group are container artifacts (LTP cannot locate the kernel .config), not real host failures; they were recorded as observed but a different host would likely classify them differently. madvise06 tbroke on missing cgroup v2 memory controller, ioctl02 on a missing tty device. 52 stale-entry candidates from prior runs remain unclaimed in the cache.
